title: The Curious Case of Estonian
bodyHtml:
Estonian is a Uralic language closely related to Finnish; it is spoken by over a million people in Estonia. In Estonian, as in many languages around the world, nouns (and adjectives) take different forms (called "cases") according to their role in the sentence. For example, in the sentence below, there are three forms of the word horse. This is similar to the difference between he, him, and his in English.

Hobunenägihobusthobusega.
horse.nominativesawhorse.partitivehorse.comitative

'A horse saw a horse with a horse.'

Estonian nouns have a lot of different forms depending on their case and their number (singular or plural). The table below illustrates various forms for different nouns and adjectives; the exact meaning of these different cases is not relevant to this problem. Be careful, however: exactly four of the forms in the table below are mistakes! Note that õ, ä, ö, and ü are vowels.

questions.promptHtml: List all four mistakes and their corrections, for example in the format printed form (case) - correct form.
questions.partPrompt: Write down the correct forms of the four incorrect words in the big table. For each one, give the form as printed, the case it belongs to, and the correct form.
questions.answerKey: laulja (partitive) - lauljat; õdel (adessive) - õel; kollaset (partitive) - kollast; suur (genitive) - suure

questions.partPrompt: Fill in the blanks in the table below.

hints.text: Do not try to learn six separate patterns. Look for columns that are simply another column plus one letter. Start by comparing the Adessive Singular with the Genitive Singular, and the Nominative Plural with the Genitive Singular, in rows you trust (such as ‘house’ and ‘nest’).

Four of the six columns can be predicted from the other two. The two "basic" forms are the Genitive Singular and the Partitive Singular: one of them plus a single consonant gives the adessive and the nominative plural forms, and the other one is the base of the Genitive Plural, which in turn plus a consonant gives the Adessive Plural. Once you have the recipes, apply them to every row: a cell that breaks a recipe in a row where the other cells agree with each other is one of the four mistakes.

Try the row for ‘road’, which is error-free. Genitive Singular tee plus -l gives the Adessive Singular teel, and tee plus -d gives the Nominative Plural teed. The Partitive Singular is teed; add -e and you get the Genitive Plural teede, and that plus -l gives the Adessive Plural teedel. Check the same recipes on ‘house’, where the Partitive Singular maja has no final -t or -d: there the Genitive Plural adds -de instead (majade).

explanationHtml:
What the columns mean

A case is a form a noun takes depending on its job in the sentence, like English he versus him versus his. You do not need to know what "adessive" or "partitive" mean here. What matters is that the six columns are related to each other by very simple rules, so most of the table is predictable from a couple of forms.

Finding the recipes

Take a row that looks completely regular, ‘house’: maja, maja, majal, majad, majade, majadel.

  • Adessive Singular = Genitive Singular + -l: maja + l = majal.
  • Nominative Plural = Genitive Singular + -d: maja + d = majad.
  • Adessive Plural = Genitive Plural + -l: majade + l = majadel.

Check these against other rows and they always hold: mehe gives mehel and mehed; põhjuse gives põhjusel and põhjused; saarte gives saartel.

The last link is between the Partitive Singular and the Genitive Plural. When the partitive ends in -t or -d, the genitive plural is that form plus -e: sööklat gives sööklate, valget gives valgete, meest gives meeste, jääd gives jääde. When the partitive ends in a vowel, the genitive plural adds -de: maja gives majade, nime gives nimede, lugu gives lugude, uba gives ubade. So the Genitive Plural tells you exactly what the Partitive Singular must look like, and the other way round.

Hunting the four mistakes (C1)

Now go row by row and see which single cell disagrees with the rest of its row. A useful trick: in each suspect row, three or four cells agree with one another and only one is the odd one out, so you correct the loner.

  • ‘singer’: the Genitive Plural is lauljate, which comes from a partitive ending in -t. But the Partitive Singular is printed with no -t. Fix the partitive.
  • ‘sister’: the Genitive Singular is õe, so the Adessive Singular must be õe + l. The printed adessive uses a different stem, so it is the mistake. Notice the Nominative Plural õed also confirms the stem õe.
  • ‘yellow’: the Genitive Plural is kollaste. Compare ‘reason’: põhjust gives põhjuste. So the printed Partitive Singular has one letter too many.
  • ‘big’: the Adessive Singular suurel and the Nominative Plural suured both point to a Genitive Singular ending in -e, but the printed genitive does not have it. Fix the genitive.

That is exactly four errors, as promised, which is a good check that you found the right ones.

Filling the new table (C2)

‘moon’. You are given the Partitive Singular kuud and the Adessive Singular kuul. Strip the -l from the adessive to get the Genitive Singular. Add -d to that genitive for the Nominative Plural. Add -e to kuud for the Genitive Plural, and then -l to that for the Adessive Plural. (The nominative plural and the partitive singular come out identical here, exactly as in the ‘ice’ and ‘road’ rows.)

‘human’. You are given the Genitive Singular inimese and the Genitive Plural inimeste. Add -l and -d to inimese for the adessive singular and nominative plural; remove the -e from inimeste for the partitive singular; add -l to inimeste for the adessive plural. This row behaves just like ‘reason’.

‘fish’. You are given the Partitive Singular kala and the Nominative Plural kalad. The nominative plural is the genitive singular plus -d, so drop the -d to get the genitive singular, then add -l for the adessive singular. Since the partitive ends in a vowel, the genitive plural adds -de (just like maja gives majade), and the adessive plural adds -l on top of that.

The big idea

Estonian looks like it has dozens of unrelated word forms, but the paradigm is built up in layers: a couple of stems, then endings stacked on top of them. Once you find which forms are the building blocks, everything else follows, and any form that does not follow is either an exception you must learn or, as here, a typo.

Points: no official per-part breakdown printed, so 2 points assigned to C1 and 0.25 to each of the twelve C2 cells (total 5). Please verify the 'sister' row of the big table (printed adessive singular õdel, which the solution flags as the error) and the 'bean' row (oa / uba / oal / oad / ubade / ubadel).
